label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
# It's one assignment

Jess texted me last night. The gist was: it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it. About half the group chat agreed with her. I started typing a reply and realized I was about to argue my case in fifteen separate texts, which is a bad way to say anything I care about. So I'm saying it here, once, and then I'll stop.

For anyone who missed the backstory: for four years at Cobb Street I've had my juniors in US History II do an oral history project on busing. Each kid interviews someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston between 1974 and 1976, records ten minutes of it, and writes a two-page reflection. I run it in both sections. In four years I'd never had a complaint.

Now I have one. A parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen, with a school committee member cc'd, saying the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it. The three of us are meeting Thursday the 19th at 3:15.

I'm not going to drop it.

Jess, I know why you said what you said, and I'm not mad about it. We met student teaching in the same building in 2012. You did this job until 2019, and now you do HR, so you've watched this kind of thing play out from both sides of the desk. You're right that I could get burned. I've had tenure since 2021, so nobody is firing me over a ten-minute recording, but tenure doesn't make my schedule and it doesn't decide who teaches AP. Halvorsen does. There are plenty of ways to make a teacher's year worse without putting anything in writing, and you know that better than anyone in the chat.

So please don't picture me being brave about this. I'm a little scared, honestly. I've just decided that being scared isn't a good enough reason.

The textbook gives busing one paragraph. That's one paragraph for something that happened in the city these kids live in, to people they eat dinner with. I can stand at the front of the room and talk about it for a week, and I do, but it stays in the same drawer as the Missouri Compromise, something that happened to other people a long time ago. The interviews are what get it out of the drawer.

In 2023 a student of mine, D., interviewed his grandmother. It turned out she drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family. He played forty seconds of the recording for the class, and when it ended nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute. I've been teaching for a while and I can't produce that silence on purpose. I've tried.

Then there's last year. A girl in my second section found out, in the middle of her interview, that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset, properly upset, and we talked after class twice. I didn't have anything wise to say. Mostly I listened while she worked out how the uncle she knew and the uncle in the story could be the same man. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year, from anyone.

I know that second story cuts both ways. It's more or less exactly what the parent is worried about, and that's the part I'd like the chat to hear, because I think a few of you assume I'm gearing up for a fight with her. I'm not. I think she has a point.

"Pressures kids" is fair. A seventeen-year-old who gets an assignment from the person who grades her isn't really free to say no. My student last year chose to keep going with it, and I'm glad she did, but I can't assume every kid would make that choice or should have to. Some families have things in them that a kid shouldn't be sent to dig up for a grade. I hadn't built in a way out, and I should have.

So the plan I'm bringing Thursday is to keep the project and add a second option. A student can interview a librarian or an archivist instead, or work from the recorded interviews from past years, with permission from the people who made them. No kid has to interview family. They'll still hear real voices from this city talking about those years, and they'll still write the reflection.

I do think the kids who are uncomfortable are the ones who need this most. I also don't get to force anyone. That's the line, and I was on the wrong side of it without noticing, and I'd rather fix that than defend it.

Where I disagree with her is "reopens wounds." I understand the feeling, but most of the people my students interview aren't being reopened. They're being asked, often for the first time. D.'s grandmother carried that for almost fifty years, and she told it to a kid with a phone because he was the first one who wanted to know.

The other thing I can't get past is "quietly." If Halvorsen wanted to argue with me about whether this belongs in the curriculum, I'd have that argument, and I might even lose it. But dropping it quietly because one email had the right person cc'd means the next email works too, on whatever comes next. And I'd have to tell next year's juniors why we're not doing the thing their older siblings did. I don't have an answer I could say out loud to them.

Jess, I'm not asking you to agree with me. You might read all of this and still think it's one assignment, and you might be right about what it costs me. I just wanted you to know I heard you, and that I thought about it properly before deciding. There's also nothing here I'm planning to torch. I'm going to walk into that meeting, tell a parent she's right about something, show her how I've fixed it, and ask to keep teaching the history of the city we all live in. If that turns out to be a firing-adjacent offense, I'd rather find out now.

Anyway. Thursday, 3:15. I'll text you when I'm out, and you can tell me you told me so or buy me a drink, depending on how it goes.
